clue.text: Charlotte races about in this?

indicators.note: about signals the letters of the two words are turned around into a new order

explanation.surface: A well-heeled Charlotte zooms around town in her big car.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the anagram and the definition: a Chelsea tractor is a jokey British name for a large 4x4 driven around posh west London, where a Charlotte might live.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase mocks the oversized off-roaders driven by wealthy urban parents on school runs, the kind of vehicle a Sloaney Charlotte would race about in.

clue.text: Meet something funny with B Ford

indicators.note: read as 'with B for D': one letter of the funny word is swapped for another

parts.note: a comedy is a funny show or play

explanation.surface: An invitation to meet a comic figure named B Ford.
explanation.walkthrough: 'B Ford' is not a name: split it as 'B for D', telling you to replace the D of COMEDY with B.
explanation.definitionFit: To come by someone can mean to encounter or call in on them, close in sense to meeting.

clue.text: NY Times singularly spreading hatred

indicators.note: spreading out the letters scatters them into a fresh arrangement
singularly asks for the plural word in its single form, dropping its final letter

explanation.surface: The New York Times is said to be spreading hatred.
explanation.walkthrough: 'singularly' turns Times into TIME; 'spreading' mixes NY with TIME to give ENMITY.
explanation.definitionFit: Enmity is active hostility or ill will, a synonym for hatred.

clue.text: Celebrity passes what sounds like ambulance during a limo trip

indicators.note: signals that the phrase for the vehicle is said aloud and spelt differently

parts.note: an ambulance is jokingly a means of sick transit, transport for the ill

indicators.note: a trip is a stumble, so these letters fall into a new order

explanation.surface: A celebrity is driven past on a limousine trip while an ambulance is heard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trip' rearranges DURING A LIMO into GLORIA MUNDI; the Latin phrase means 'thus passes the glory of the world'.
explanation.definitionFit: Celebrity is glory or fame, and the Latin motto says that worldly glory passes away.

clue.text: Range in the Arabian desert

indicators.note: in signals the letters sit inside the run of the next two words

explanation.surface: Something stretches across the Arabian desert.
explanation.definitionFit: The Andes is the long South American mountain range.

clue.text: See 1
In train wreck, old Sophocles?

indicators.note: In tells you to set the word for old within the shuffled letters
a wreck mangles the letters of train into another order

parts.note: aged means old

explanation.surface: An ancient Greek playwright involved in a railway disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wreck' scrambles the train letters, and 'In' sets the word for old among them; the question mark marks Sophocles as one example of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Sophocles wrote tragedies, so he is an example of a tragedy writer; the question mark flags the example.

clue.text: Wrong to be suspicious with a promotion

indicators.note: in a down answer a promotion lifts the letter higher in the word

parts.note: wary means suspicious or on guard

explanation.surface: Getting a promotion makes someone suspicious that something is wrong.
explanation.walkthrough: 'promotion' moves the A of WARY up a place in this down entry, giving AWRY.
explanation.definitionFit: Awry means amiss or gone off course, so wrong.

clue.text: Pony went bust worth not much money

indicators.note: bust means broken, so the letters break up and re-form

explanation.surface: A pony has gone lame and its value has crashed.
explanation.definitionFit: Something twopenny costs two pence, so it is cheap and almost worthless.

clue.text: Drive to evaluate Spooner's lily pad?

indicators.note: points to swapping the opening sounds of two words, after the Reverend Spooner

parts.note: lily pad describes a rest for a toad, so lily stands in for the frog-like creature
a pad is a place to rest

explanation.surface: A test drive to judge a lily pad, the Spooner way.
explanation.walkthrough: A lily pad is a 'toad rest'; swapping the first letters gives ROAD TEST.
explanation.definitionFit: A road test is a trial drive used to assess a vehicle's performance.

clue.text: Copy of Two Thousand and One, with music finale

indicators.note: Two asks for the thousand-and-one pair to appear twice

parts.note: M is the Roman numeral for a thousand
I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: a finale is the end, so the closing letter of music

explanation.surface: A copy of the film 2001 with its musical finale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Two' doubles MI (thousand and one in Roman numerals) to give MIMI; the 'finale' of music is C.
explanation.definitionFit: To mimic is to imitate, so to copy.

clue.text: Runs out of air? Oh dear!

indicators.note: out of order: the letters come out jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone runs out of breath and groans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of' jumbles AIR OH DEAR. 'Runs' looks like a verb but is a slang noun.
explanation.definitionFit: The runs is slang for loose bowels, a colloquial term for this condition.

clue.text: Supports bar locks

parts.note: bar means except, as does but
locks of hair are tresses

explanation.surface: Bars that lock things also hold them up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bar' is the preposition meaning except, not a rod.
explanation.definitionFit: Buttresses are structures built against walls to prop them up.

clue.text: Tie the knot after most excellent love is given

indicators.note: after places the marrying word at the end of the build

parts.note: best means most excellent
love is zero in tennis, the letter O
to tie the knot is to wed

explanation.surface: A couple marries once the finest love has been given.
explanation.definitionFit: Bestowed means conferred or presented as a gift.

clue.text: Are you, as they say, taken in by strong Arab commander leaving home course?

indicators.note: taken in by puts the spoken letters inside the word for strong

parts.note: fit means strong and healthy

indicators.note: as they say flags that the words are heard rather than spelt

parts.note: these two words spoken sound like two letters

indicators.note: leaving drops the word for home from the commander's name

parts.note: Saladin was the Muslim sultan who fought the Crusaders
in means at home

explanation.surface: A question for a strong Arab leader who has left home on a course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as they say' turns 'Are you' into its text-speak letters, 'taken in by' the word for strong; 'leaving' drops the word for home from Saladin, the twelfth-century sultan.
explanation.definitionFit: Fruit salad is a dessert, which is a course of a meal.

clue.text: Get some sleep before family calls for tableware

parts.note: to nap is to get a little sleep
kin are relatives
rings means phones or calls

explanation.surface: Taking a nap before relatives phone about dishes.
explanation.definitionFit: Napkin rings hold rolled serviettes on a dining table, items laid with the place settings.

clue.text: Starts to put record straight about some current spoilers

indicators.note: about puts those initials around the unit word
the opening letters of the next three words are taken

parts.note: an ampere is a unit amount of electric current

explanation.surface: Setting the record straight about plot spoilers in current affairs.
explanation.walkthrough: The initials P, R, S go 'about' AMPERE: P + AMPERE + RS.
explanation.definitionFit: Pamperers indulge others excessively, and so spoil them.

clue.text: Endlessly going off on tirade is not clever

indicators.note: off means awry, so the remaining letters are rearranged
endlessly removes the final letter of the word

parts.note: a rant is a tirade

explanation.surface: Banging on endlessly in a tirade is not a clever look.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endlessly' trims the last letter of going and 'off' scrambles what is left; 'on' is a link placing the tirade word after.
explanation.definitionFit: Ignorant means lacking knowledge, loosely uneducated or dim.

clue.text: Website tribute about the centre of Aleppo

indicators.note: about wraps the tribute word around the central letters

parts.note: homage is a tribute

indicators.note: the centre of a six-letter word is its middle two letters

explanation.surface: A website pays tribute to the heart of the Syrian city of Aleppo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the centre of' a six-letter word is its middle pair, and 'about' wraps the tribute word around them.
explanation.definitionFit: A home page is the main or front page of a website, standing for the site itself.

clue.text: See 3
Life in Paris before Napoleon evacuated a capital city

parts.note: vie is French for life

indicators.note: evacuated means emptied, leaving only the outer letters

explanation.surface: Parisian life before Napoleon emptied a capital.
explanation.definitionFit: Vienna is the capital of Austria.

clue.text: Scarcity put right inside 28

indicators.note: inside puts the letter for right within the cross-referenced word

parts.note: the answer to 28 across is DEATH, the end of the linked phrase

explanation.surface: Scarcity puts right the problem in another clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A dearth is a shortage or lack, which is scarcity.

clue.text: See 12
Each letter is liberal

parts.note: per means for each, as in per head
a missive is a letter

explanation.surface: Each letter is liberal in its views.
explanation.definitionFit: Permissive means tolerant and lenient, a synonym for liberal in attitude.

clue.text: 'Head off, bottom up' as a slogan

indicators.note: in a down answer, up means the letters are read from the bottom
head off removes the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A cheeky slogan: off with your head and bottoms up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head off' makes OTTOM, which 'up' turns round in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A motto is a short phrase expressing a guiding principle, much like a slogan.

clue.text: Surgeon's first working rule: man, I like the aortic valve!

indicators.note: first takes the opening letter of the surgeon word
working signals the letters are put to work in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A surgeon's enthusiastic rule of thumb about heart valves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first' gives the surgeon's opening letter and 'working' scrambles the next three words; 'like the aortic valve' describes rather than names it, as an adjective should.
explanation.definitionFit: The aortic valve has half-moon-shaped cusps, so it is called a semilunar valve.

clue.text: An underground place of humiliation

parts.note: an is the indefinite article, here giving just A
a basement is a room below ground level

explanation.surface: An underground dungeon where people are humiliated.
explanation.definitionFit: Abasement is the act of being lowered in dignity, so degradation or humiliation.

clue.text: See 24
19 artist's work to fade out ultimately, such a recipe for disaster

parts.note: 19 down is VIENNA, and Gustav Klimt, a Viennese painter, made the famous work The Kiss

indicators.note: out means wrong or off, so these letters are reordered
ultimately points to the last letter

explanation.surface: A painter's work fading away is a disaster.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges TO FADE into OFDEAT, and the last letter of such adds H.
explanation.definitionFit: The kiss of death is an idiom for something that seems helpful but brings certain ruin.

clue.text: See 27
